cues.en: I would like to end this chapter with the best practices that apply to the user management.
So when we have users or groups, the best practices are that we should prefer groups in order to manage
privileges.
Imagine the following scenario.
Let's say we have somebody who's creating online courses and let's say I want to give somebody else
read access to my online courses.
Then I could do this for this user.
But.
Let's say, for example, I would need two people that would work for me and that would help me create
those online courses.
Then I would have to change the permissions and it would be a lot of effort.
If I were using groups from the beginning, that would be really easy.
I could just add those users to the groups and they would have access to my online courses.
So this is why we should prefer groups.
The next thing is that we should try to use meaningful group names so that the groups are really descriptive
and the names really describe what those groups do.
This will help us to keep having a nice overview over all the groups that we are having.
The next thing is that we should try to follow the principle of least privilege.
So that means that we should only assign users only to the necessary permissions or the necessary groups
that they actually require.
We should not assign additional privileges to them.
So we should avoid the use of overly permissive access rights.
The next thing is that we should really be careful whether we want to give right access to people because
then they can change scripts or they can change the files there and this can be potentially problematic.
The next point that I would like to mention is that we should try to minimize the number of users with
elevated privileges.
Again, we should try to reduce the attack surface.
The next thing is that when we use group memberships, of course we need to be careful that we keep
them up to date.
So, for example, if somebody would help me with my online courses here and then he would leave my
company or he would no longer work for me, then of course I should update the group memberships and
take away the rights so that he or she cannot or can no longer access my materials.
So yeah, that's part of the regular review for groups permissions.
So when you use those groups to manage those permissions, all of this will be possible for you.
And it will also be possible that when a new team member comes in that you can just give them the rights
that he or she needs.
So you can see how user management works on Linux, how you can manage groups, how all of that fits
together with the file permissions and how you can use the sudo command to temporarily allow users to
have elevated permissions.
So you see how all of that fits together.
And you can use this to set up your system in a way that those users that should have access to specific
resources are allowed to.
But others who should not have access to those resources are not having access to those.
So this is how all of that works.
